Maladaptive Strategies.value: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
I am permanently an outsider now

vignette: Samira had spent thirty-two years behind the reinforced doors of the state correctional facility, her Middle Eastern heritage and steady demeanor making her a quiet pillar among her peers. But at sixty-eight, her certainty shattered during a routine perimeter shift when a sudden, unnatural quiet fell over the yard. The stillness lasted only three seconds before a group of men breached the lower gate, and Samira remembered sprinting toward the newer intake coordinator who stood near the opening. Her instincts had frozen at the critical moment; she watched helplessly as the man was dragged behind the concrete wall, and when she finally reached the control room, her hands were too uncoordinated to override the lock. The incident left her with a clinical assessment that quietly confirmed what her body already knew. Her conviction that she had fundamentally failed to protect the coordinator now shaped how she interpreted the world; that lingering guilt turned every moment of unusual silence into a precursor to violence, and made her body react before she had time to think. Her belief that she was permanently an outsider, combined with her conviction that she had failed, drove her to drop the administrative duties that required her to work alone and to surround herself with staff chatter in the break room just to stay safe from her own thoughts. Because she was certain she had been helpless, her nervous system began to anticipate danger long before she had time to process it. Her body would seize and her breath would shorten at the drop of a lunch tray, which pushed her toward constant checking of every exit and corridor. She found herself scanning the yard for anomalies and avoiding the solitary stretches of the lower tiers. The more she monitored the environment and clung to noise, the more certain she became that people simply could not be trusted with the truth of her vulnerability. That feedback loop tightened with every passing month. Scanning the yard for threats and filling her hours with constant socialising only deepened her isolation, making her feel like a stranger in her own career and confirming her belief that she had failed the very people she worked to keep safe. Her husband noticed how she woke at the slightest creak of the house settling, how she paced the kitchen until dawn, and how her reliance on crowded dinners made her exhausted. Her reliance on crowded dinners and constant socialising kept her body in a state of permanent readiness, which shattered her sleep and made her react to every shifting shadow as an imminent attack. The more she leaned on noise and company, the more she convinced herself that her own instincts had been fatally flawed, and that isolation was the very space where danger waited. What finally brought her to my office was not the nightmares, but the morning she stood frozen at her apartment door, refusing to leave her husband because the hallway felt too quiet. She sat across from me with hands still tracing the edges of her purse, hoping someone could help her untangle the guilt that had kept her so deeply afraid. She desperately wanted to stop feeling like a stranger in her own life, and to sleep through the night without bracing for the next breach.
